mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes GLK 320 CDI or 350 CDI V6 engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A rebuilt OM642 engine for the GLK 320 CDI costs £3,800-£4,900 supply-only; a rebuilt OM642 engine for the GLK 350 CDI costs £4,000-£5,300 supply-only. Fitting adds £700-£1,300 depending on complexity - V6 work requires specialist knowledge.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of OM642 oil cooler seal failure on a Mercedes GLK 320 CDI or 350 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: A burnt-oil smell after highway driving or oil pooling in the V of the engine is the classic warning sign. The oil seals themselves are a £10 item; the labour to replace them is about £900 at a specialist. If ignored, coolant contamination leads to bearing washout and terminal engine seizure.

mainEntity.name: Is the Mercedes GLK 350 CDI V6 engine (OM642) reliable?

acceptedAnswer.text: The OM642 V6 is a fundamentally strong and refined engine - the 3.0-litre V6 turbodiesel found across Mercedes' SUV and van range. It has one famous weak point: the oil cooler seals. With upgraded Viton seals fitted, these engines routinely exceed 150,000 miles.

mainEntity.name: How long do Mercedes GLK 320 CDI and 350 CDI V6 engines last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Properly maintained OM642 V6 engines routinely reach 150,000-200,000+ miles before major work is needed. With upgraded Viton oil cooler seals fitted, these engines demonstrate exceptional longevity.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in my Mercedes GLK 320 CDI or 350 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if the GLK is otherwise in good condition with no rust or major electrical or transmission faults. A rebuilt OM642 costs £3,800-£5,300 - comparable to or less than replacing a £4,000-£12,000 vehicle, especially when factoring in the cost of finding a comparable replacement SUV.

mainEntity.name: What oil does my Mercedes GLK 320 CDI or 350 CDI V6 need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mercedes-Benz specifies low-SAPS oil meeting MB 229.51 or 229.52 - typically 5W-30. The OM642 V6 requires approximately 8.0 litres with filter.

historyTimeline.h2: Mercedes Benz GLK Class 320 CDI/350 CDI - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The GLK 320 CDI launched with the X204 generation in 2008 as the flagship diesel, powered by the OM642 3.0-litre V6 turbodiesel producing 224hp. In April 2009, the GLK 350 CDI replaced it with an updated 231hp V6, followed by a 265hp BlueEFFICIENCY version for the 2012 facelift. These V6 diesels represented the pinnacle of GLK diesel performance, offering refined V6 power and exceptional towing capability.

milestones.description: OM642.930, 3.0L V6 diesel, 224hp @ 3,800rpm (GLK 320 CDI 4MATIC, X204 launch)
April 2009 - OM642.832, 3.0L V6 diesel, 231hp @ 3,800rpm (GLK 350 CDI 4MATIC, replaces 320 CDI)
OM642.835, 3.0L V6 diesel, 265hp @ 3,800rpm (GLK 350 CDI 4MATIC BlueEFFICIENCY, facelift)
2015 - GLK 350 CDI continues as the flagship diesel to end of production

commonProblems.h2: Mercedes Benz GLK Class 320 CDI/350 CDI Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The OM642 V6 diesel is a fundamentally strong and refined engine - the 3.0-litre V6 turbodiesel that powered the flagship GLK diesel models. However, it has one famous weak point: the oil cooler seals. The factory seals sit deep in the valley between the cylinder banks. Heat cycles harden them, and they begin to seep. Turbo seals are also notorious for causing major issues if leaks aren't addressed. Every rebuilt engine supplied through EnginesMarket includes upgraded components - Viton oil cooler seals and reinforced turbo seals - addressing these original failure points, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited mileage warranty.

problems.h4: OM642 Oil Cooler Seal Degradation - The V6 Diesel's Famous Weak Point
problems.rootCause: The OM642's oil cooler sits in the tight valley between the V6 cylinder banks, directly under the turbo and intake plumbing. Factory rubber seals harden with heat cycling, allowing oil to pool in the valley or drip onto the exhaust, producing a burnt-oil smell. The oil seals themselves are a £10 item - the labour is the cost. If ignored, coolant contamination leads to bearing washout and terminal engine seizure.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Engine valley access, remove intake crossover, turbo and swirl manifold; replace with upgraded Viton seals, new oil cooler, gaskets
repairOptions.longevity: If caught early with no other damage; Viton seals resolve the design flaw

repairOptions.tier: Major - EGR cooler + swirl flap replacement (while open)
repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace EGR cooler, swirl flap motor and linkage, intake manifold gaskets
repairOptions.longevity: Best performed while oil cooler seals are being replaced - saves duplicate labour

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete V6 swap with upgraded Viton oil cooler seals, new EGR cooler, bench-tested bottom end, 12-month warranty
repairOptions.longevity: If oil contamination has caused bearing damage

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical 2008-2015 GLK 320 CDI or 350 CDI 4MATIC is worth approximately £4,000-£12,000 depending on mileage and condition. The GLK 320/350 CDI sits in the £4,000-£12,000 band - replacement cost is typically justified for well-maintained examples with good bodywork and transmission health.
problems.recommendation: The OM642 oil leak is progressive, not sudden. If caught early during routine servicing - oil pooling in the valley or a burnt-oil smell after highway driving - the specialist seal overhaul at £900-£1,400 extends engine life affordably. The oil seals themselves are a £10 item; the labour is the cost. Once coolant has entered the oil pan or metallic debris is present, patch repairs are futile. For high-mileage GLK 350 CDI models, a rebuilt OM642 delivers superior long-term value and peace of mind - specialist pricing of £3,800-£5,300 is significantly lower than dealer rates.

problems.h4: OM642 EGR Cooler & Swirl Flap Failure - Emissions and Performance Issues
problems.rootCause: The EGR cooler can become blocked with carbon deposits, restricting exhaust flow and causing emissions warning lights. The intake swirl flap motor and linkage also wear over time, throwing codes like P2004-P2006. These components sit in the same valley area as the oil cooler, making it cost-effective to address them together.

Doing both together saves you paying the same teardown labour twice. On a GLK 320/350 CDI worth £4,000-£12,000, this combined approach is cost-effective preventative maintenance.

problems.group: OM642 Turbo Seal Failure & Injector "Black Death"
problems.h4: OM642 Turbo Seal Failure & Injector "Black Death" - Power Loss and Rough Running
problems.rootCause: Turbo seals are notorious for causing major issues if leaks aren't addressed. The copper sealing washers under CDI injectors can also fail, allowing combustion gases to escape past the injector body. The leaking gases bake into a hard, tar-like carbon crust around the injector - "Black Death." Left long enough, the injector becomes welded into the head.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace copper sealing washers, clean injector bore, leak-off test
repairOptions.longevity: If caught early before injector seizes

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace turbo oil seals, inspect turbo shaft play, clean EGR system
Specialty pullers, head work, injector seat machining
repairOptions.longevity: If injector has seized and requires extraction

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete V6 swap with new injectors, seals, turbo components, 12-month warranty
repairOptions.longevity: If turbo debris or seized injectors have caused damage

problems.vehicleValueCheck: As above - a typical GLK 320/350 CDI is worth £4,000-£12,000.
problems.recommendation: Turbo seals and injector seal leaks are progressive issues. If you notice a chuffing sound from the engine bay at idle or a diesel-exhaust smell inside the cabin, have the injector seals inspected immediately. Caught early, resealing an injector is a £250-£450 per cylinder job. Caught late, extracting a seized injector can require specialty pullers and head work. For turbo seal issues, replacement at a specialist is significantly cheaper than a full turbocharger replacement.
